title: Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 20 Oct 2026]
Title:Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Long-horizon terminal agents may solve a task in one run yet fail across repeated runs. Stochastic errors can propagate through actions and context, creating a gap between capability and reliable execution. We present RiseHarness, a framework for iteratively improving agent harnesses with model weights fixed. It focuses on flipping tasks with both successful and failed runs under the same configuration, using successful runs as references for failure analysis. RiseHarness combines agent trajectories with internal harness traces from a runtime monitor to examine how model actions interact with command execution, feedback, context management, and completion decisions. A Harness Handbook links this evidence to harness behaviors and source code, helping identify recurring problems in mechanisms shared across tasks. RiseHarness then searches other harness frameworks for relevant implementations and adapts them as design references to the current model and execution protocol. Candidate changes undergo behavioral checks and repeated task evaluation; versions with measured gains seed the next iteration. This loop integrates suitable mechanisms from different frameworks into a single harness and uses new execution evidence to guide further changes. We evaluate task success and reliability across models, ablate harness execution evidence and external research, and test transfer to unseen benchmarks with the same model. RiseHarness treats a specific model as the unit of harness adaptation, studying how changes to shared interaction mechanisms can make existing capabilities more reliable across tasks.

report.summary: RiseHarness proposes automated, model-weight-fixed harness evolution to make long-horizon terminal agents reliable by learning from mixed success/failure runs.
report.background: Terminal agents are LLM-driven systems that plan, run shell commands, read feedback, manage context, and decide when to stop. Their performance depends not only on model weights but on the harness: prompts, tool interfaces, execution loop, error handling, memory, and completion logic. Long-horizon tasks compound small stochastic errors, so an agent may succeed once but fail on repeat runs. This capability-reliability gap has become central as labs ship coding and computer-use agents and benchmarks such as Terminal-Bench and SWE-bench reward multi-step execution. Most improvements still come from better models or manual scaffolding. RiseHarness sits in a growing line of work on agent harness engineering: keep the model fixed, instrument execution, and automatically revise the surrounding software. It also reflects a broader shift from prompt tweaking toward systematic, evidence-driven optimization of agent runtimes.
key_points: The paper targets the reliability gap between one-off success and repeatable execution. It focuses on “flip tasks” that both pass and fail under the same configuration, using successful runs as references to diagnose why failures occur and which harness mechanisms are fragile.

RiseHarness combines full agent trajectories with internal harness traces from a runtime monitor. A Harness Handbook links this evidence to specific harness behaviors and source code, helping identify recurring problems in shared mechanisms such as command execution, feedback handling, context management, and completion decisions.

Instead of only editing the current harness, the system searches other agent frameworks for relevant implementations and adapts them to the current model and execution protocol. This lets it borrow proven design patterns rather than invent every fix from scratch.

Candidate changes are gated by behavioral checks and repeated task evaluation. Only versions with measured gains seed the next iteration, creating an iterative loop that integrates useful mechanisms and uses new execution evidence to guide further changes.

Model weights stay frozen; the harness is adapted per model. The paper evaluates task success and reliability across models, ablates execution evidence and external research, and tests transfer to unseen benchmarks with the same model.
report.impact: RiseHarness shifts attention from raw model capability to the software layer around the model. For the AI industry, it suggests harness engineering can be automated and evaluated like a product, potentially improving reliability without retraining. For developers, it offers a blueprint for tracing failures, borrowing patterns across agent frameworks, and gating changes with repeated tests—but also warns of benchmark overfitting and added runtime complexity. For regular users, the payoff is terminal agents that complete multi-step tasks more consistently, with fewer silent failures. The risk is that model-specific harness tuning becomes opaque and brittle; teams will need transparent traces, safety checks, and transfer testing before trusting autonomous shell access.
report.tools: Watch the RiseHarness paper for code release; pair it with Terminal-Bench and SWE-bench for repeated-run reliability tests. OpenHands, SWE-agent, and Aider are useful reference harnesses for tool loops, context management, and command feedback. For runtime tracing, evaluate LangSmith, Arize Phoenix, or AgentOps to capture harness traces. OpenAI Codex CLI and Claude Code are commercial terminal-agent harnesses worth comparing, but check their telemetry and sandboxing.
